text:
anya: Quick RFC follow-up — connection-priority plumbing at the edge. Question: do we prefer an early-accept model (frontdoor returns/starts streaming immediately while backend token refresh/validation runs async) vs deferring accept until auth/refresh completes? Latency win vs wasted work / side-effect risk. Thoughts?

sam: Early-accept is tempting for p50 latency, but worried about billing + rate-limit accounting. If we stream data and the refresh fails later, how do we signal the client? Hard to reconcile with retries. :thinking:
ravi: Also side-effects. If a call triggers downstream writes and we later abort because token refresh failed, we risk partial commits. For read-only flows maybe ok, writes are scary.

lex: Can we do a hybrid? Allow early-accept only for routes marked idempotent/read-only. Add a short "soft admit" header that indicates the response is provisional until auth-confirmation arrives. If final auth fails, we close with a trailer indicating revert/abort.

anya: Draft idea: header `x-rw-frontdoor-admit: soft` (or `strict`). trailers: `x-rw-auth-final: ok|fail`. Frontdoor still needs to surface an abort trailer for clients that support trailers.
mike: Practically: many clients don't support trailers or will ignore midstream aborts. Early-accept + hedging may double-stream same work if we hedge to another backend — cost increases. Maybe limit early-accept to small responses or short TTL streams.

kat: Observability is critical. We should tag spans with `edge.auth.window` and emit metrics for "admit-then-revoke" counts so SLOs can reflect wasted tokens.
sam: Implementation note — our current edge runtime couples auth middleware with the stream multiplexer. We should decouple: an "admit" phase that performs syntactic checks and allocates stream slot, and an async "validate" phase that can close the stream with an auth trailer or let it continue. That reduces blocking in the main accept path.

lex: Example route policy sketch (very rough):
{
  "route": "/v1/embeddings",
  "early_accept": "soft", // values: "off", "soft", "strict"
  "max_stream_size_bytes": 65536,
  "require_no_sideeffects": true
}

ravi: Strong +1 on the "require_no_sideeffects" flag. We also need a way for downstream services to declare idempotency semantics and for platform to maintain a whitelist of safe routes.

anya: Edge cases: 1) long-lived streams (minutes) — early-accept risks long wasted GPU time if validation fails midstream. 2) billing reconciliation — if we charge per-token, we might need a refund path for aborted streams. 3) retries/hedging interactions — duplicated work.
mike: For long streams we should default to `early_accept: off` unless route explicitly opt-in. For short responses or guidance endpoints we can be permissive.

kat: Observability + billing: include a "revoke_reason" tag on aborted streams and export it to billing pipeline so we can reconcile and possibly not bill customers for aborted tokens during experiments.
deploy-bot: deploy scheduled: branch=feature/edge-auth-split env=staging at=2026-03-24T08:00:00Z (experiment: early_accept=soft on /v1/generate-preview)
ravi: SG. I'll add the whitelist and a quick test harness to simulate token refresh failures and measure "wasted token" rate.

anya: Action items: 1) I will draft a short RFC PR with header/trailer semantics + route flag. 2) Run the staging experiment (thanks @deploy-bot) and measure p50/p95 and abort-rate. 3) Instrument traces/metrics and hook billing reconciliation. I'll post RFC by EOD tomorrow.

lex: :thumbsup: I'll add unit tests for idempotency and a mock client that verifies trailer handling.
mike: One last ask — add a kill-switch per-tenant so we can quickly disable early-accept if we see regressions.

anya: Good call. Adding tenant kill-switch to RFC checklist. Thanks everyone.
__notes: thread discussing early-accept vs deferred auth at edge, header/trailer semantics, route flags, observability, rollout
